#6559. The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6557. Black Holes and Their Mysterious Bright Structures Explained

Astrophysical jets launched from black holes aren't shy. They announce their presence with enormous blasts of energy that extend extreme distances into space. They're the most long-lasting and luminous sources of electromagnetic energy in the Universe.

Supermassive black holes (SMBH) emit the largest astrophysical jets, and they come from active galactic nuclei (AGN) which are SMBH that are actively accreting material. As material gathers in an accretion disk around a SMBH, it rotates and heats up. Some of the material is ejected out of the black hole in the powerful jets.

These jets are impossible to ignore. No astrophysicist could feign their interest. Exactly how these powerful expressions of cosmic energy are created isn't clear, though some things are known.

Astrophysicists know that they're powered by a SMBH's rotational energy and their extremely powerful magnetic fields. They know that they move at relativistic speeds. And they know that they can inject gigantic amounts of energy into the intergalactic medium, heating up gas and introducing turbulence, two things that act against star formation.

One thing that puzzles researchers is how the different regions in a black hole jet have different brightnesses. The expectation is that the center of the jets would be brightest, because this is where energy is most concentrated. But when researchers examine the jets coming from the SMBH in Centaurus A, the closest radio galaxy to Earth, that's not what they see.

Since it's so close and so bright, Centaurus A is one of those natural laboratories for extreme physics that makes astrophysicists' eyes light up. They've been observing the jets in Centaurus A in detail for many years. Observations with the Event Horizon Telescope spanning a decade have revealed that its jets are brighter at their edges than in their centers, in a phenomenon called limb brightening. Why is that?

New research in Astronomy and Astrophysics has an explanation. It's titled "Probing anisotropic particle acceleration and limb brightening in Centaurus Aâs jet." The lead author is Felix Glaser, Master's student at the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg in Germany.

"Relativistic jets are among the most fascinating phenomena in the universe, and recent high-resolution very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations, including the Global mm-VLBI Array and the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), are able to resolve their structure close to their launching site," the authors write. The combined observations show the black holes with brighter limbs are not only found in Centaurus A, but in M 87 and 3C 84, too.

This image shows four different looks at the central region of M 87. The top image from the Hubble is in visible light. The other three are all in polarised light. The lines mark the orientation of polarisation, which is related to the magnetic field in the regions imaged. Though the researchers focused on Centaurus A, this image highlights how magnetic fields and polarity influence astrophysical jets. Image Credit: EHT Collaboration; ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), Goddi et al.; NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); VLBA (NRAO), Kravchenko et al.; J. C. Algaba, I. MartÃ­-Vidal

Each of these three galaxies are different from one another, making it difficult to understand the cause of their limb brightening. "Therefore, as a pilot study, we aimed to model the EHT observations of Cen A," the authors explain. It's the closest, so that makes sense.

This is a composite image of Centaurus A, with the individual images and their wavelenghts on the right. The image is from the Hubble (visible), Chandra (X-ray), Spitzer (infrared), and the Very Large Array (radio). Image Credit: NASA, CXC, SAO, Astrophotography by Rolf Olsen, NASA-JPL, Caltech, NRAO, AUI, NSF, UOH, M. Hardcastle

The researchers performed a magnetohydrodynamic simulation of an accreting supermassive black hole and how it launched it jets to observe the plasma dynamics involved. Since these jets are relativistic, the simulation included general relativistic effects. They also adjusted their simulation to match the properties of Centaurus A. "In order to match our model to the EHT observations, we adjust several free parameters..." the authors write, including black hole mass and the viewing angle.

The simulation successfully mimicked the recent observations of Centaurus A with the EHT.

"Our results demonstrate that the edge-brightening observed in Cen A can be naturally reproduced by an anisotropic particle distribution," the researchers write.

That means that the electrons emitted in the jets aren't distributed evenly over pitch angles. Pitch angles are the difference between the magnetic field and each electron's velocity. This is where synchrotron radiation enters the picture. Synchrotron radiation is when particles are forced to follow the curve of a magnetic field.

The emission of synchrotron radiation is strongly dependent on the pitch angle. So as a result, the observed brightness of the radiation changes depending on the viewing angle of the magnetic field the particles are forced to follow.

This figure from the research shows the synthetic polarized intensity images of our Cen A model at four representative frequencies: 86 GHz (panel A), 230 GHz (panel B), 680 GHz (panel C), and 3 THz (panel D). Each one zooms in closer and shows more detail in the model. Image Credit: Glaser et al. 2026.

âWhat is truly amazing is that microscopic plasma effects can shape structures on vastly larger scales,â said Dr. Christian Fromm, leader of the Computational Astrophysics Group. âFuture observations will reveal even more of these plasma signatures, making it increasingly important to include realistic plasma physics in our models already today and to further investigate the highly nonlinear effects of relativistic plasma.â

This figure shows how microscopic plasma effects can shape the large-scale structure of black hole jets. The hot accretion flow surrounding the supermassive black hole is shown in red, the relativistic jets in blue, and the magnetic field structure by gray helical field lines. Colored particles and arrows illustrate the motion of accelerated particles along the jet. Top right: The Event Horizon Telescope image of the inner jet of Centaurus A at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. Bottom right: The synthetic EHT observation generated from the new plasma-informed model. (Image Credit: Christian M. Fromm, Janssen et al. 2021 and Glaser et al. 2026)

âCen A is our closest window into the physics of relativistic jets,â said lead author Glaser. âThe fact that our plasma-informed model reproduces the observed edge brightening suggests that we are capturing an important piece of the underlying physics. These processes may not be unique to Cen A, but could be common in relativistic jets throughout the Universe.â

This study makes real progress in understanding the details of astrophysical jets, and how they exhibit things like limb brightening. It links the small scale of plasma physics with the jets and their characteristics. It's all because of a focused, multi-disciplinary effort.

âBy bringing together expertise in high-resolution observations, numerical simulations, and plasma physics, we are making progress toward understanding how black holes launch powerful jets and how these jets produce the radiation we observe. The new study is an excellent example of this approach,â said Fromm.

New telescopes are coming online that will take this work even further. The Square Kilometre Array will be the world's largest and highest-resolution radio telescope when it comes online in 2027. Updates to the Very Large Array will also drive progress when they're completed in 2031.

This work may affect more than our understanding of black hole jets. On a detailed plasma physics level, there are similarities between the jets and fusion. If we ever have a functioning fusion reactor, it will involve extremely powerful artificial magnets to generate powerful fields that confine the plasma.

This illustration shows some of the "D"-shaped toroidal field magnets in the ITER international nuclear fusion research and engineering project being built in France. Each magnet weighs 330 tons, and their job is to confine the plasma inside ITER's vacuum vessel. Lessons learned by studying plasma physics in black hole jets are applicable to fusion reactors. Image Credit: ITER Consortium.

âA black hole and a fusion reactor may sound like completely different worldsâbut both are governed by the physics of plasma,â says Professor Karl Mannheim, holder of the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg. âAt Centaurus A, we can study plasma under conditions that cannot be created on Earth. These insights not only help us understand the Universe, but may also contribute to the development of future fusion energy.â

#6556. Computer Simulations Provide the Best Explanation for Those "Little Red Dots" Yet!

When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. These galaxies were bright and red - earning them the nickname Little Red Dots (LRDs) - and far more abundant than cosmological models predicted. Scientists theorized that these were early quasars, galaxies with active galactic nuclei (AGNs) powered by the "seeds" that would grow to become supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

However, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Big Bang. This led scientists to consider various theories, compact collections of stars, "dusty" galaxies, supermassive stars, and "black hole stars." While the more recent Direct Collapse Black Holes (DCBHs) theory offered the most compelling argument to date, new simulations by an international team of astronomers indicate that they may be the remnants of collapsed supermassive primordial stars.

The study was led by Dr. Daniel Whalen from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation. His colleagues included researchers from United Arab Emirates University, the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the Institute for Astronomy and Royal Observatory at the University of Edinburgh, and the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA). The paper detailing their findings was published in the The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The little red dots could represent galaxies in an evolutionary phase predating the luminous quasar phase. Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/ISTA)/ETH Zurich/NAOJ

Previous attempts to explain the rapid formation, abundance, and spectral characteristics of LRDs all suffered from the same issue. While each explained some characteristics, none could account for everything the JWST revealed in its deep field surveys. Then came the DCBHs theory, which argues that SMBH seeds formed directly from massive clouds of cold gas. While this theory did fit Webb's observations nicely, it still faces numerous theoretical and environmental challenges.

For starters, the core premise of the DCBH theory is that a massive cloud of cold gas could collapse under its own gravity. However, gas tends to fragment into smaller clouds as it cools, leading to a cluster of primordial (Population III) stars instead of a black hole seed. To prevent fragmentation, the gas cloud must remain hot, requiring a very specific amount of Lyman-Werner (LW) radiation from a synchronized star-forming galaxy in its vicinity to destroy the main coolant - i.e., molecular hydrogen (Hâ).

This raises additional problems, including the self-shielding nature of molecular hydrogen. As a gas cloud becomes increasingly dense, its outer layers absorb the LW radiation, shielding the inner core. This means that the critical amount of radiation required to suppress cooling across the entire cloud would be much higher. Even if the SMBH seed did manage to form, the radiative pressure it would emit (plus mechanical feedback from the disk and jets) would slow the accretion rate, significantly slowing further growth.

Whalen and his team found another explanation borne out by advanced cosmological simulations. As he said in a University of Portsmouth press release:

LRDs have been one of the most surprising discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope. They are compact, only a few hundred light-years across, but are as bright as much larger galaxies, and their unusual V-shaped spectra have defied the usual astrophysical explanations. Their lack of detectable X-ray and radio emissions has left astronomers struggling to explain what they are.

Artist's impression of a galaxy forming stars within powerful outflows of material blasted out from supermassive black holes at its core. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser

Based on their simulations, the team produced a model showing that LRDs are most likely galaxies with AGN powered by massive black holes that formed through the collapse of supermassive primordial stars. What's more, their model suggests that the black holes are largely concealed by dense, massive discs of the gas that created them. These gaseous envelopes trap high-energy X-rays while allowing some visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light to escape, which fits with the unusual light signatures detected by the JWST.

The simulations also explain another long-standing mystery about LRDs: that a large cluster of stars in the disks of these small galaxies produces the blue part of the spectrum Webb observed. These disks, according to the models, contain around 100 million stars densely packed into regions measuring only 500 light-years in diameter, matching what astronomers observed in LRDs. Based on the available data, the team further concludes the black holes at the center of these primordial galaxies are only about 10 million Solar masses.

This is a few orders of magnitude less than previous estimates, which indicated a maximum of 100 million Solar masses. While this research is unlikely to be the final word on the nature of LRDs, it offers what is (to date) the most fitting explanation that matches the observations. "What makes this discovery so exciting is that we may be witnessing the birth of the first supermassive black holes," said Whalen. "For decades, simulations have predicted that these objects should exist, and now the James Webb Space Telescope may finally be allowing us to see them."

Further Reading: University of Portsmouth, The Astrophysical Journal Letters

#6555. The Maldon Salt Scandal, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.)

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a new study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its big flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

#6554. The Absolute Best Pie Recipes, According to Eater Staff

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

#6553. Microscopic Space Dust Reveals A Hidden Reservoir Of "Heavy Water" Beyond Neptune

Astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects. That was certainly the case recently when twelve dust grains collected by a high-altitude aircraft helped solve a mystery about the birth of our Solar System. Or at least that is the argument in a new paper published in Science Advances by researchers at NASAâs Johnson Space Center and UCLA. According to the paper, the region beyond Neptune once had a massive isolated reservoir of âheavy waterâ that never mixed in with the inner planets.

In this context âheavy waterâ doesnât mean the type formed with deuterium, like the kind used in nuclear reactors. Instead, it refers to a heavier version of the other element in good old H2O - oxygen. Most of the universeâs oxygen atoms are an isotope called oxygen-16, with eight protons and eight neutrons. However, a small percentage weighs in a bit heavier - oxygen-17 and oxygen-18, which carry an extra neutron or two, respectively.

In 2011, NASAâs Genesis mission caught particles in the solar wind that showed the Sun housed an overwhelming amount of regular oxygen-16. However, Earth, Mars, and the asteroid belt seemed to have much more of the heavier oxygen isotopes. Which meant thereâs a mismatch between what we see inside the Sun and what the planets were formed out of. Scientists have been attempting to explain why for years.

Fraser explains the important of cosmic dust to life on Earth.

The most common explanation of why is known as carbon monoxide self-shielding. Around 4.5 billion years ago, when our Solar System hadnât fully formed yet, ultraviolet light from the Sun blew apart carbon monoxide molecules at the outer edges of the protoplanetary disk of gas and dust. Because oxygen-16 was the most prominent in the disk, the carbon monoxide particles that were made out of it would absorb much of the UV light that was directed at the disk, breaking the ones that were closest the light source (i.e. the Sun) apart. They eventually reformed with hydrogen to make âregularâ water.

However, that left other wavelengths of UV free to travel into the farther reaches of the protoplanetary disk. And some of those wavelengths were particularly good at breaking apart carbon monoxide molecules that had formed with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. So, in the outer disk, those heavier isotopes made up a higher percentage of the free-floating ions that eventually bonded to hydrogen, in their case creating âheavyâ water.

That makes sense from a theoretical standpoint at least, but proving this âheavy waterâ reservoir exists has been tricky. Almost all the meteorites we have found were formed in the main asteroid belt - not far enough out to capture particles of the reservoir. Some cometary sample missions, such as Rosetta and Stardust, have tried to capture water samples from these ambassadors of the outer solar system, but their method of capture resulted in the water-bearing materials melting, leaving no trace of their isotopic configuration.

Enter the new paper. Lead author Lindsay Keller and his team turned to interplanetary dust particles (IDPs). These microscopic grains are formed when comets and other icy bodies out in the Kuiper belt, the area past Neptune, collide and break apart. Some of the grains that result from those collisions are pulled inward by the Sunâs gravity, eventually intersecting the orbits of the inner planets - including Earth.

During their journey, they are subjected to extreme amounts of high energy particles from solar flares, which leaves microscopic scars on them called solar energetic particle tracks. Previous studies had proven that one way to prove a piece of dust had traveled from the Kuiper Belt is that have around a hundred times more energetic particle tracks, due to their much longer time in interplanetary space, than particles from asteroids do. In other words, if you can count the radiation tracks, you can prove whether a grain of dust came from beyond Neptune or not.

That is exactly what they proved with twelve dust grains collected during NASAâs Cosmic Dust program - an ongoing airborne sampling program running out of Johnson Space Center since 1981. Shockingly, the collected particles still had lots of clays, like saponite, which are made with water, as well as iron-nickel sulfides and around four times as much carbon as would be expected for a primitive meteorite. The minerals proved that liquid water once flowed inside its parent Kuiper Belt object, either heated by radioactive decay or the kinetic energy of another impact.

Using a specialized microscope, the researchers measured the exact oxygen isotope ratios in the clays in the samples. They then worked back through chemical modeling to determine the original recipe for the water on the parent rock that formed the grains. They found that the primordial Kuiper Belt objects these grains came from were extraordinarily enriched with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18 - definitively proving that the reservoir of heavy water does exist out beyond Neptune.

Fraser talks about how there was liquid water on the asteroid Ryugu.

As a consequence, they also, tangentially, provided a significant bump to the carbon monoxide self-shielding theory. And also noted the similarities to a specific unusual meteorite known as Acfer 094, which they hint might actually be a meteor from the Kuiper Belt itself. But there was one final mystery the paper needed to resolve - if there was all this heavy water out in the outer solar system, why didnât it migrate in when the planets were forming?

The authors offer a simple explanation - Saturn. As Saturn grew in the early solar system, its gravity created a high-pressure ridge in the protoplanetary disk, acting as an invisible barrier to keep lightweight material from being pulled too far in towards the Sun. So, thanks to around a dozen specks of dust, we now have a more clearly defined picture of what our solar system looked like in the very early days of its formation - and it seems we can thank our giant ringed neighbor for some of how Earth ended up with its current isotopic balance.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. #6550. 37 Thanksgiving Cocktails and Drinks for Every Guest

Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle. There are the cranberry, apple, and maple flavors we crave this time of year, plus big-batch drinks that won’t keep you playing bartender all afternoon. We’re talking freezer-ready martinis, bourbon punch, and a cranberry mule that guests can spike themselves. After all, your to-do list is long enough.

And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether. When dinner gives way to dessert, warm up with a hot buttered rum, mulled wine, or spiced apple cider. Just don’t forget to set out a few Thanksgiving appetizers while you’re at it.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

We love a Paper Plane as much as the next discerning cocktail drinker, but shaking them up one at a time? Hard pass. Batch the bourbon, Aperol, and amaro for this Thanksgiving cocktail ahead, then stir in the lemon juice and water about an hour before serving.

The “upside-down” refers to the inverted ratio of gin and vermouth in these martinis (not what they’ll do to you). The result is a lighter-drinking cocktail you can batch ahead and stash in the freezer until guests arrive.

All the steeped, spiced flavors you love in a hot toddy, with none of the warmth. This icy twist keeps pre-dinner cocktail hour refreshingly chill. Relatives, take note.

Apple cider, tart cranberry juice, and spicy ginger ale give rum punch a seasonal makeover. Make the cranberry-studded ice cubes ahead of time; they’ll keep the punch cold and make each glass look party-ready.

Sure, a cold beer works fine while you're watching football or tending the turkey fryer. But a pitcher of crisp Mexican lager punched up with margarita citrus makes the occasion feel a little more festive. For another low-effort beer cocktail, try a Spaghett—just lager, Aperol, and lemon.

For a big-batch cocktail with a distinctly autumnal spin, combine rum with dry hard cider and fruit. Prepare the rum base ahead, but save the bubbly cider until just before serving to preserve its fizz.

Bourbon, cognac, floral Earl Grey tea, and an herb-honey syrup make a party-ready punch. For an eye-catching presentation, add an ice ring decorated with lemon slices and rosemary sprigs.

Mezcal, orange liqueur, honey, and chocolate bitters make a lightly smoky cocktail that's particularly good with dessert. Even better, you can batch eight servings and stash them in the freezer up to two weeks ahead. No last-minute shaking required.

Feeling a little gung-ho about Christmas’s fast approach, are we? A big-batch punch packed with cranberry, citrus, nutty sherry, and warming spices makes a delicious bridge between Thanksgiving and the winter holidays.

A seasonal riff on the French 75 swaps gin for bourbon and adds a homemade pear syrup spiced with cinnamon, ginger, and cloves. We like it for a sparkling toast before dinner or alongside pie afterward.

The season of Hallmark’s flannel-clad himbos calls for a drink to match. Enter this lower-ABV sipper made with apple cider and amaro. A little bitter, a little sweet, and just fizzy enough—rather like the male lead in whatever movie “your aunt” is watching.

Homemade cranberry-thyme syrup gives this sparkling cocktail its ruby-red glow. A little Campari adds a pleasantly bitter edge, while Champagne makes it worthy of a holiday toast. The syrup can be prepared up to two weeks ahead.

If you want to start Thanksgiving with a little bubbly, this three-ingredient, lower-ABV aperitif is a fine place to begin. The recipe serves four, and the ginger syrup can be made well in advance.

Replace the gin in a classic Negroni with sparkling wine and you’ve got a lighter, fizzy aperitif. The bubbles mellow Campari’s bitter edge, making this a friendly introduction for the Negroni-curious.

Two ingredients, one very good drink. Fino sherry and ginger ale make a lightly boozy, pleasantly dry cocktail with just enough ginger bite.

Botanical gin, bittersweet grapefruit, and sparkling sake make a bubbly cocktail that’s bright enough to cut through a rich Thanksgiving spread. It serves six, so you can pour a round without mixing drinks one by one.

We love a margarita riff no matter the season. Ginger and rosemary bring a distinctly autumnal edge to this fizzy version, with just enough sparkle to make it feel like a holiday toast.

No punch bowls, cocktail shakers, or complicated mixology required for this two-ingredient drink. You’ve got better things to do between hosting duties and getting all those Thanksgiving sides to the table.

A lower-ABV sipper is your friend during a long day of polite frivolities. The Adonis sounds hella sexy, and we love the earthy nuttiness of sherry and sweet vermouth, made spritzy with club soda.

On a holiday where cranberries overflow-eth, pour a drink to match. Tart, citrusy, and just sweet enough, this vodka cocktail gets its signature pink hue from cranberry juice. A bright counterpoint to all that rich Thanksgiving food.

A classic old-fashioned needs just bourbon or rye, sugar, and bitters. Making drinks for a crowd? Follow our big-batch old-fashioned method to prep ahead and avoid playing bartender all Thanksgiving.

Think of this as an apple-brandy riff on the Manhattan. Sweet vermouth rounds out the fruit’s warmth, making this a particularly fitting fall cocktail.

Not quite a whiskey sour, not quite a cider cocktail, this autumnal drink mixes apple brandy with lemon and orange juices, maple syrup, and a dusting of nutmeg. It tastes like fall without leaning too heavily on baking spices.

Impress your whiskey-loving dad with a Prohibition-era cocktail he may not have heard of. Juicy grapefruit and floral honey give bourbon a bright, citrusy lift, just as winter citrus season is getting underway.

Bourbon, lemon juice, and simple syrup make a tart, boozy drink that’s just sweet enough. It’s ideal for anyone with a minimally stocked bar and a preference for the classics.

Think of the Boulevardier as the Negroni’s bourbon-loving cousin. Whiskey takes the place of gin, bringing warmth and richness to the bittersweet combination of Campari and sweet vermouth. A fine choice for sipping before dinner.

A smoky mezcal cocktail with Earl Grey tea syrup and grapefruit liqueur, this bright, aromatic margarita riff is an intriguing choice for Thanksgiving brunch—or for guests who prefer tequila to bourbon at cocktail hour.

A homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail a distinctly Thanksgiving twist. Lime juice keeps it tart, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim adds a fragrant finish. Make the jam ahead to streamline cocktail hour.

Whether for your Thanksgiving pregame or tomorrow morning’s hair of the dog, a well-made Bloody Mary is always welcome. Worcestershire, horseradish, hot sauce, and fresh lemon give this savory classic its signature kick.

A packed to-do list is no match for this make-ahead drink. Simmer red wine, cider, fruit, and spices ahead of time, then add tawny port and gently reheat when your guests arrive. Keep it warm in a slow cooker for self-service away from the kitchen.

We’d welcome a pot of mulled apple cider at any fall gathering. It’s nonalcoholic, serves a crowd, and fills the kitchen with the scent of warming spices. Guests can add a tipple of brandy, bourbon, Calvados, or rum if they wish.

Can’t decide between hot cider and spice-rich chai? Have both. This cozy, nonalcoholic drink brings tea and warming spices to apple cider, making it a particularly good companion for a second slice of pie.

For those who’d rather drink their Thanksgiving dessert, a warm mug of dark rum, butter, sugar, and spices delivers the goods. It’s rich, fragrant, and an excellent reason to linger at the table after the pie plates are cleared.

Blood orange, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves make this sweet-tart, nonalcoholic drink feel right at home on Thanksgiving. Prepare the shrub ahead, then top with sparkling water when guests arrive.

Who says a nonalcoholic spritz can’t have a little attitude? A bittersweet alcohol-free aperitif and a splash of olive brine give this savory, citrusy drink plenty of complexity. Serve it very cold, with an olive garnish.

Green tea, lemon juice, fresh mint, and honey make a soothing tonic after the Thanksgiving bacchanal. Alcohol-free on its own, it can take a splash of mezcal if anyone wants to steer it into cocktail territory.

Spiced maple syrup and cranberry juice reimagine the typical Moscow mule as a Thanksgiving drink that skips the vodka. Note that Angostura bitters contain alcohol; for a completely alcohol-free version, use an alternative like All the Bitter.

#6549. Fermi’s 14-Year All-Sky Map Bridges Astronomy’s Elusive "MeV Gap"

Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. Weâve always had trouble measuring them in the âmega-electron voltâ (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the âMeV gapâ. But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration recently published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20-200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray observatory, that can capture radiation at the x-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher end ones.

But why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit rather than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

At high energies - around 1 giga-electron volt (GeV), the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, at the lower 20-200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from. Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide - more than forty times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the Sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

However, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data thereâs some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical, and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects - 325 of them - are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consist of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nuclei. FSRQs represent a type of âblazarâ - a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy at this 20-200 MeV spectral window.

Fraser and Pamela discuss the differnet "colors" of gamma rays.

Closer to home, the catalogue includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars - the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time itâs ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, are the 73 sources that donât have a clear counterpart at other energies. 60 of those appear to be brand new gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the dataset awaiting follow-up observations. One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China, and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data of this satellite, which was originally launched in 2008. However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASAâs Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2-5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades worth of Fermi might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.

#6548. Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity. Unlike stars like our Sun, which are relatively radio-quiet, red dwarfs (M dwarfs) can produce strong radio emissions. A team of astronomers used that to their advantage to take precision measurements of a binary pair of M dwarfs about 59 million light years from Earth. They determined the stars' orbits and masses with uncommon accuracy.

One fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger. Stars inherit angular momentum from their formation in gas clouds, and since M dwarfs are so small, that momentum is concentrated, making them spin rapidly. They eventually slow down, but this initial rapid rotation makes them very active.

The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.

One subset of young M dwarfs is even more extreme. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. They're M dwarfs that display complex, periodical optical light curves with sharp drops rather than smooth drops found in most stellar light curves. Their drops aren't simple; there can be multiple dips and peaks during a single rotation. Astrophysicists call their light curves multi-harmonic, and the patterns repeat across multiple rotations.

This image shows CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. Notice the sharp drops in the curves rather than typical smooth drops found in other stellar light curves. Image Credit: Bouma et al. 2023. AnJ

The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star. Though CPV stars have complex light curves generated by their youthful, rapid rotation, their youthfulness also means they're radio loud. In fact, since both of these stars are young M dwarfs, they're both radio loud. That helped the researchers measure them with such accuracy.

The measurments of DG CVn are in new research in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Accurate dynamical mass and orbit determination of the M dwarf binary DG CVn using astrometric very long baseline interferometry." The lead author is Paul VLBI , a network system engineer at the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry ERIC (JIVE), and a Leiden Observatory PhD student. It's noteworthy that this is the first mass measurement of a system with a CPV star.

"We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star." - Boven et al. 2026.

The astronomers' results are based on observations that spanned 18 years. Observations with the National Science Foundationâs Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) between 2023 and 2025 were especially important in their precise results. The VLBA is a system of 10 radiotelescopes across the USA, each one measuring 25 meters. The 10 dishes work as an interferometer, and the VLBA has the longest baseline in the world, up to 8,611 km long.

"Astrometry through very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) allows the monitoring of radio-loud stars and the detection of any reflex motion due to stellar or substellar companions," the authors write. Reflex motion is the characteristic gravitational wobble induced in a star when a companion tugs on it.

That wobble is often used to detect unseeable exoplanets orbiting stars. Even a small planet can make its star wobble, and that's at the heart of the radial velocity method of detecting exoplanet. The DG CVn system was actually found when astronomers were searching for exoplanets with the radial velocity method. But the system exhibited a more powerful and complex wobble than an exoplanet would.

âWe were really lucky to hear about this object when we had developed tools with which we could explain these motions,â said Boven. âBut the real surprise came when we also detected the second radio-loud dwarf in the observations we did to confirm our model. It really allowed us to measure the system very precisely.â

Measuring reflex motion accurately with the VLBI let the astronomers track the stars' paths, including the tiny wobbles, which in turn let them understand the mass of the stars with extreme precision.

This figure from the research shows the VLBI detections of both members of DG CVn, and their modeled motion across the sky. The dates mark the predicted positions of DG CVn B over time. The inset image shows recent observations when both sources were detected. Image Credit: Boven et al. 2026. A&A.

"In our recent observations, we reliably detected both binary components," the authors write. "A unique and accurate determination of the 1647.647 Â± 0.027 day orbit, with a parallax distance of 18.1851 Â± 0.0033 pc (about 59 light years), is presented. The dynamical masses were estimated with a precision of 0.16% from the sampled posteriors."

The pair of stars orbit each other every 4.511 years on an elongated elliptical orbit. When they're closest to one another, they're only separated by 0.59 astronomical units. DG CVn A is the more massive of the pair with 0.39 solar masses, while DG CVn B has 0.36 solar masses. The pair is close enough to measure their distance with parallax, which gives accurate measurements.

The red dwarfs and their radio emissions are central to this work. The stars are simply too close together from this distance to be separated in optical observations. But the VLBA can pinpoint their locations with extreme accuracy. All of this work let the researchers characterize the system in clear detail, following the motions of both stars through the sky separately.

âDG CVn is a beautiful example of what precise radio astrometry can reveal,â said Jay Blanchard, NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory astronomer and study co-author. âBy following these two stars over many years, we can see their orbital motion directly and use that motion to determine properties that would otherwise be extremely difficult to measure.â

These accurate measurements also tell astronomers about their planetary systems. Planets form in protoplanetary disks around stars, and since these stars are so close together, that limits the size of their disks. Smaller disks mean smaller planets, so that limits the size of any exoplanets in the system. It's also extremely unlikely that any long-period planets are orbiting either star.

According to the researchers' estimates, an exoplanet in orbit around one of the stars could only be in a stable orbit if its orbital period was less than approximately 23 days. For a circumbinary planet orbiting both stars, the orbital period would have to be at least about 36 years. These approximations are also important, because they can refine the understanding of how exoplanets can form and survive in binary star systems.

Gaia's Data Release 4 is due in a couple of weeks, and it will include binary star parameters for the mission's complete survey. But that data alone won't be able to differentiate between binaries where both are low mass stars, and binaries where one might be a massive planet. But the VLBI will be able to address that. "Astrometric follow-up of selected detections with VLBI can help to differentiate between binary star systems and reflex motion due to large exoplanets (or even both)," the authors write.

"We have presented a complete binary orbital solution with high accuracy based on VLBI astrometry of a binary that is difficult to resolve for optical telescopes on the ground or in orbit," the authors write. "The absolute astrometry provided by VLBI allowed the individual dynamical masses to be determined with high accuracy. These results show that VLBI is well suited for studying the orbits of radio-loud stars."

The results also show how powerful the combination of archival observations and new observations can be. "The value of combining archival and recent VLBI astrometric observations has been demonstrated. It resulted in a highly accurate determination of the system composition, orbit, position, and distance," the authors write. "We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star."

The VLBI network of radio dishes is about to have a growth spurt when the Square Kilometre Array and the Next Generation Very Large Array come online. That will improve the system's reach and precision.

"In the future, we hope to make measurements precise enough to detect planets in orbit around such radio-loud dwarfs,â said Huib van Langevelde, chief scientist a the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry and Leiden Observatory professor. âWe think that when the ngVLA and the SKA become part of the VLBI network, we can do even more precise measurements, for many more, more distant stars.â

#6547. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

#6546. Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

Unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is currently a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

SwRI - SwRI team studies interior composition, origins of ice giants

O. Mousis et al - Primordial and Radiogenic Argon 40 in Uranus and Neptune

UT - Argon â The First Noble Gas Molecules Discovered In Space
