#6522. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

The common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

This simple graphic shows how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112

This is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

Observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in new research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag."

That much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

Astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â said first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â

Stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.)

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â

âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

This is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel shows the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026)

Since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an important role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

As in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an important role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

That work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

The astronomers called the pair Big Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

These artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia)

"The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

"In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory says that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

But this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

This work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

#6519. NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

The spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”

Navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

Didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

These conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

Rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

During this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

That day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

The experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

However, the results also raised important questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

The spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an important role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

#6517. Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun

It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

The key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve said before, is energy transfer. How does the pathway work for energy to come from the Sunâs interior to its upper atmosphere? At this point, the accepted answer seems to be through massive magnetic fields pushing plasma outwards and heating it intensely, but the nuances of the exact mechanism remain hazy.

Dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot. But up until now we have had difficulty tracking where exactly they go, largely because the Sun is so bright it's hard to isolate individual tendrils from the overall burning mass of plasma.

Fraser attempts to answer why the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface.

To do so, Guotang Wu and Xiaoli Yan of the Yunnan Observatories at the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined data sources. They used the New Vacuum Solar Telescope, located in southwestern China, to monitor a sunspot in an active region of the Sun known as NOAA 13182. Crucially, they did so for just over an hour on January 10th, 2023, and took snapshots of the chromosphere â the middle layer between the Sunâs surface and its outer atmosphere â every 45 seconds. They then combined these ground observations with data from Chinaâs CHASE solar satellite and NASAâs Solar Dynamics Observatory, providing a multi-layered and multi-spectral view of this active sunspot.

Over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes. Even during that time, they manage to stretch on average 1,130 kilometers â roughly the distance from New York to Chicago.

So where do those jets come from in the first place? Sunspots are already famous for creating features known as ârunning penumbral wavesâ of compressed gas that move across the halo surrounding the sunspotâs core. According to math described in the paper, the rhythmic pulsing of the fibrils almost matches the five-minute cadence of the running penumbral waves in the sunspot. This, in turn, points to another underlying phenomena â magnetoacoustic waves.

Fraser talks about the highest resolution image ever taken of the Sun.

Under the surface of the Sun, hot convection cells of plasma constantly vibrate features known as âmagnetic flux tubesâ, creating low-frequency sound waves that leak upwards into the chromosphere. As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. However, these breaking waves are not like those of water â each breaking wave is accompanied by a miniature sonic boom known as a magnetoacoustic shock. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils.

Buried in the data there was a clear pattern of how much the orientation of these magnetic fields matters for the creation of fibrils. When the magnetic field lines point straight up, the plasma jets experience stronger deceleration and pulse at shorter intervals. Whereas when the fields lean more horizontally across the Sunâs surface, the fibrils decelerate more gently and pulse over longer periods. This confirmed a long-standing theory about how magnetic tilt affects solar sound waves.

To tie all this back to the original theme â extreme coronal heating â observations from SDO revealed corresponding signatures in gas heated to hundreds of thousands or even millions of degrees. So, the plasma pushed up by those shockwaves doesnât just appear to fizzle out - it directly transfers energy into the corona itself, which aligns with what many of the recent papers on this topic have been proving in various ways.

But weâre still not 100% sure of some of the nuances of how this complex magnetic dance actually works. That might have to wait for even bigger ground-based telescopes such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which can resolve the magnetic threads inside these massive jets. But until then, we have an even clearer picture of how an acoustic hum plays a role in stoking the inferno of the Sunâs outer atmosphere.

#6516. A Triple Star System 'That Shouldn't Exist,' Only 28 Light-Years from Earth

Sometimes astronomers search for one thing and find something completely different. There are many examples of that, from the Cosmic Microwave Background to Pulsars to Gamma-Ray Bursts. The same thing happened recently to researchers who were hunting for exoplanets. Instead of distant planets orbiting a distant star, they found an unusual triple star system in our stellar neighbourhood.

Their unexpected discovery is presented in a paper titled "WelopÅâai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. An international team of researchers made the discovery, and the lead author is Ãtienne Artigau. Artigau is from the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âWe were actually looking for planets,â lead author Artigau said in a press release. âInstead, we found something much more surprising.â

IREx is the group behind Canada's contribution to the JWST, the FGS/NIRISS instrument. IREx's other instrumentation projects include the SPIRou and NIRPS high-precision infrared spectrographs, installed in Hawaiâi and Chile respectively, and the GPI imager on the Gemini-South telescope. This discovery began with the SPIRou (SpectroPolarimeter Infrared) instrument, which uses the radial velocity method to detect exoplanets tugging on their stars.

But in this case, instead of finding an exoplanet tugging on a star, they found another star tugging on a star.

"Serendipity has long played a key role in astronomy, offering insights into new phenomena," the researchers point out. "We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf WelopÅâai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou," the authors write in their paper. "The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc."

Astronomers have watched the M dwarf, named IRAS 21500+5903 (also called TYC 3980-1081-1 A), and known about its unusual radial velocity (RV) signal since 2019. In this work, the researchers used SPIRou to gather almost five years of RV data on the red dwarf. That data showed that the RV signal had a large amplitude, which was inconsistent with an exoplanet signal. Exoplanets produce small wobbles as they tug on their stars.

"The mid-M dwarf showed a near-constant acceleration of approximately 5 m sâ1 dâ1 (â¼1800 m sâ1 yrâ1), a level inconsistent with a planetary companion: on a few-year orbit around a 0.42 Mâ star, even a Jupiter-mass planet would induce an acceleration of at most â¼40â130 m sâ1 yrâ1," the authors write.

That's math-speak for saying that the RV signal is up to 45 times stronger than a planet the mass of Jupiter could produce.

This figure shows the RV curve of WelopÅâai Aa from SPIRou observations spanning 4.8 yr, with the best-fit Keplerian model overplotted. The inset shows one week of observations, and shows how precise the measurements were. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321

Astronomers already knew that the M dwarf had a binary companion. It's a white dwarf, the massive dead core of a star that was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But that star is too far away to be responsible for the RV signal. Instead, another massive white dwarf was most likely close to the M dwarf.

âThe objectâs unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,â said co-author Charles-Antoine Parent, a Mastersâ student at the University of Montreal. âThe most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldnât be ruled out.â

To narrow it down, the researchers turned to the Gemini North Telescope and its âAlopeke instument. âAlopeke is a high-resolution imager that can eliminate distortion caused by Earth's atmosphere.

âAlopeke revealed the nature of the third star in the system, showing that it was a second white dwarf that forms an inner pair. "This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au (Pâ>â1000 yr) from a previously known white dwarf," the authors write.

These panels show Alopeke observations in three different epochs, with yellow arrows showing the new white dwarf's position in December 2023 and 2024. It's more visible in some channels than others. The M dwarf is the central bright spot or region, it's shape distorted in the effort to highlight the white dwarf. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321

Determining the mass of a solitary white dwarf is challenging. There are billions of them in the galaxy, but precise mass measurements of them are very rare. Only a handful of masses have been determined for nearby white dwarfs. Determining their masses in binary stars is easier, and because the new white dwarf interacts gravitationally with the red dwarf, the researchers could determine its mass dynamically, rather then depending on its brightness or its spectrum.

They found that the new white dwarf companion has about 0.62 solar masses. "The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level," the researchers explain.

The system has been named WelopÅâai, a Hawaiian word that combines welo (an inherited or family trait) and pÅâai (an orbit or encircling path), together evoking a âpath of family traits.â The primary red dwarf is designated WelopÅâai Aa, its newly discovered close white dwarf partner is WelopÅâai Ab, and the outer white dwarf is WelopÅâai B.

This graphic shows observations of the WelopÅÊ»ai triple-star system, located only 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: WelopÅÊ»ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and WelopÅÊ»ai B, a second white dwarf much farther away. The image on the right is a close-up view of the inner pair, and it shows the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) that was detected with the Gemini North telescopeâs âAlopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the starsâ orbital paths. Image Credit: Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF

This system is very unusual, and rare. By determining its mass so accurately, the discovery will inform models of stellar evolution, something astrophysicists are always keen to improve.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises.â - Ãtienne Artigau, IREx, University of Montreal.

The new white dwarf was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But since it's so close to the red dwarf, the pair most likely interacted gravitationally at earlier stages of the white dwarf's evolution. It's possible that the two were inside a common envelope at one point, a situation where an envelope of gas surrounds both stars. That often forces the stars to spiral inward and merge. That should have destroyed WelopÅÊ»ai A, the red dwarf. But it appears to be intact, which is surprising. Somehow it survived that disruptive, turbulent scenario and follows a stable orbit.

âThe system should not exist,â says Prof. Patrick Dufour, white dwarf specialist at UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al and co-author of the study. âWe have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.â

There are still some unexplained things about this system. The red dwarf is between 9 and 11 billion years old, yet is suprisingly metal-rich. Stars this old aren't expected to have such high metallicity. "Reproducing the metallicity would require the M dwarf to have captured roughly two-thirds of the metals, and almost none of the hydrogen or helium, ejected by the inner WDâs progenitor," the authors write, and there's no known mechanism that could do this.

"These puzzles, together with the still-open question of how the inner binary avoided a classical common-envelope in-spiral, identify WelopÅâai as a valuable benchmark for future work on binary-star pollution and tidal evolution," the authors write.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,â said Artigau. âEven when weâre searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us!â

#6515. What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya

#6514. An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a New Era of Optical Computing

Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.

For decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work. Now, researchers in South Africa have discovered that a magnetic field can also affect light when it points sideways across a fiber, challenging an assumption that has guided optical engineering for more than 50 years.

The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them. It may also offer a new way to control light for optical computing.

MSc student Mohammed Raiyan Sharif and Professor Mitchell Cox at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg demonstrated the previously overlooked interaction, known as the transverse Faraday effect. Their research was conducted at the Wits Optical Communication (OC) Lab in the university’s School of Electrical and Information Engineering.

Optical fibers carry internet signals through thin strands of glass, but they can also detect magnetic fields. This sensing ability relies on the Faraday effect, first observed by Michael Faraday in glass in 1845. When a magnetic field points along the direction light travels, it slightly rotates the light’s polarization, or the direction in which its electric field oscillates. Measuring that rotation can reveal the strength of the magnetic field and the electrical current producing it.

A sideways magnetic field was not expected to produce the same effect. To investigate, Sharif and Cox placed strong magnets beside a stationary multimode optical fiber without touching it, then watched the light emerging from the other end.

Multimode fibers have relatively wide glass cores that allow light to travel along many different paths, repeatedly reflecting off the core’s mirror-like boundary. At the output, the overlapping waves create a pattern of bright and dark spots called speckle, similar to the shifting patterns inside a kaleidoscope.

As the researchers rearranged the magnets, a camera recorded changes in that pattern. The sideways magnetic field was somehow altering the light’s behavior inside the fiber.

“It wasn’t hard to 3D print a rig to test our intuition. Working out the theory for what we were seeing was the challenging part,” says Sharif. “The key was to return to the underlying equations and question assumptions that are usually taken for granted in fiber optics.”

The explanation involved a small part of the light wave that a widely used mathematical shortcut ignores. Known as the weak-guidance approximation, this approach assumes that light’s electric field oscillates almost entirely across the fiber, leaving out a tiny component that oscillates along its length.

The approximation works extremely well when the fiber’s core and surrounding glass have similar refractive indices, which describe how strongly a material slows light. However, Sharif and Cox tested step-index fibers, where the refractive index changes abruptly at the core’s boundary rather than gradually, as it does in graded-index fibers.

When that difference is large, the normally neglected longitudinal component becomes significant near the core’s edge. By including it in their equations, the researchers showed that a sideways magnetic field transfers some of the light’s transverse oscillation into the longitudinal component. This changes how light reflects inside the fiber and, ultimately, the speckle pattern it produces.

The team also distinguished the new interaction from the Cotton-Mouton effect, another response to sideways magnetic fields. The Cotton-Mouton effect increases with the square of the magnetic field’s strength, while the transverse Faraday effect increases in direct proportion to it.

Their measurements confirmed four predictions. The effect disappeared without a sufficiently strong step in refractive index, became stronger when light entered at steeper angles, occurred for only one polarization relative to the magnetic field, and varied with wavelength in the same way as the conventional Faraday effect.

With a magnetic field of 0.24 tesla, roughly the strength found close to a powerful neodymium magnet, light polarized across the field produced a speckle pattern only about 84% similar to the original.

“What is surprising is finding an overlooked, useful interaction in such a familiar technology,” says Cox. “It’s quite exciting that there is always something new to learn or discover, and often these things are right under our noses, hidden in the assumptions we have made for decades.”

One possible application is monitoring electrical currents with fibers laid alongside cables, including those buried in trenches. However, magnetic fields near most cables are much weaker than those used in the experiment, so the sensitivity of a practical sensor remains uncertain.

The researchers also envision replacing permanent magnets with electrical coils, allowing currents to control the patterns of light traveling through a fiber.

“Besides sensing, I think that being able to control different modes (patterns of light) inside the fiber electrically could unlock a new way to do optical computing,” says Cox. “We can model the way light gets distorted when it propagates through fibers, frosted glass windows, or even the atmosphere. If we change our perspective on those models, we can actually use light to do mathematical computations for us, for free.”

Reference: “Transverse Faraday effect in multimode fibers” by Mohammed R. Sharif and Mitchell A. Cox, 30 September 2026, Optics Letters. DOI: 10.1364/OL.611078

The research was supported by the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the National Research Foundation (NRF).

#6512. A Radical Theory about the Universe Just Passed Some Key Tests. So... What Does that Mean?

By the 1970s, scientists largely accepted the theory that the Universe was permeated by a dark, invisible mass that prevented galaxies from flying apart. While scientists had speculated about the existence of "Dark Matter" for years, it was the work of Vera C. Rubin that made it official. By the 1990s, deep field observations made by the venerable Hubble Space Telescope led scientists to theorize that there was a powerful cosmic force driving expansion, what would come to be known as "Dark Energy."

These two theories have become part of the predominantly accepted model of the Universe, known as the Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ÎCDM) model. However, alternative theories, like the Covarying Coupling Constants plus Tired Light (CCC+TL), still endure. Between 2025 and 2026, researchers at the University of Ottawa (go GeeGees!) tested the CCC+TL model against a range of important astronomical observations. The model passed these tests, challenging what we think we know about the Universe.

The research was conducted by Rajendra Gupta, an Adjunct Professor in uOttawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras. As they described, they tested the CCC+TL model against the predicted abundance of certain elements (hydrogen, helium, and other light elements) shortly after the Big Bang, using cosmic-chronometer measurements. Their results are detailed in a paper published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

The cosmic Dark Ages refer to the first one billion years after the Big Bang and before the formation of the first stars and galaxies. Credit: NASA

While scientists have observed considerable indirect evidence for Dark Matter and Dark Energy (DM and DE), no direct detections have been made, despite decades of research. In addition, the ÎCDM model has faced challenges in recent years, as observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) revealed an abundance of mature galaxies in the early Universe. This has led to renewed interest in alternative theories such as Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and CCC+TL.

The latter model suggests that what is usually attributed to DM and DE could instead come from evolving fundamental constants that govern how forces and particles interact. In particular, CCC+TL changes Einstein's field equations for General Relativity (which describes gravity) and the FriedmannâLemaÃ®tre (FL) equations that describe cosmic expansion (aka. the Hubble-LemaÃ®tre Constant). Moreover, it uses the ages of galaxies to estimate how fast the Universe has expanded over time. As Gupta summarized:

Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations. A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.

For their simulations, Gupta and Samaras couldn't simply modify standard computer models; they had to develop CCC+TL-compliant equations and code. As they describe in their paper, the model's results agreed with several major observations. They further applied the model to the 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and found that it reproduced their rotational curves without dark matter. They also applied it to the famous Bullet Cluster, a pair of merging galaxy clusters from which Rubin derived much of the evidence for DM.

In this case, the extra gravitational effect predicted by the CCC+TL model was consistent with observations of the clusters, which the researchers consider an early proof of concept. Alongside Utkarsh Kumar, a postdoctoral researcher in observational cosmology at uOttawa, Gupta and Samara applied the model to observations of time dilation in supernovae. Their results are described in a separate study that is still pending review. In another study, Gupta proposes that observations attributed to DM and DE likely originated from covarying coupling constants.

Age comparison against redshift in CCC+TL and ÎCDM models. Credit: uOttawa/Gupta et al. (2026)

In the standard model, the Universe was only about 300 million years old when the first stars and galaxies began forming, a period known as Cosmic Dawn. Under CCC+TL, the Universe would have been about 4.6 billion years old during this period, which would be long enough for the early galaxies observed by Webb to have formed and matured. In summary, the CCC+TL model suggests that we live in a Universe much older than 13.8 billion years, placing its age at around 26.7 billion years.

Upcoming observations will offer additional opportunities to test this new model. For example, there's the General Observations (GO) GO 3293 GLIMPSE program, or the Gravitational Lensing and NIRCam IMaging Program to probe Early galaxy formation and Sources of reionization. This ultra-deep observation program will use the JWST's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) and gravitational lensing from the Abell S1063 galaxy cluster to study early galaxy formation and cosmic reionization. Said Gupta:

Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies. We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached. The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ÎCDM limits.

A recent satellite photo captured an underwater cloud of fish sperm, or milt, appearing to glow green during a Pacific herring spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along the coast of Canada's Vancouver Island.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada [48.95586624, -125.42994277]

What's in the photo? A green cloud of milt (fish sperm) and eggs during a Pacific herring spawning event

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This surprising satellite snap shows a giant underwater plume of fish sperm that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The colorful cloud appeared during a spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along Canada's western coastline.

The striking sight was spotted in Barkley Sound, along a section of the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, roughly 45 miles (70 kilometers) north of the U.S. border. The bright-green cloud is the most concentrated between Salmon Beach — the triangular town in the center of the image — and the smaller Forbes Island, which is also "glowing" along its northern coast.

The green cloud is around 4 miles (7 km) from end to end and is made of milt — a fluid containing sperm made by fish, mollusks and other aquatic animals — that was released during a Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii) spawning event. Like many other fish species, Pacific herring reproduce by congregating in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt, which disperses over the area and fertilizes the eggs.

Pacific herring, which grow to around 10 inches (25 centimeters) long, often congregate in this spot off Vancouver Island in late winter or early spring, gathering for several weeks before releasing their gametes, or sex cells, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

"The herring spawn is a really fabulous time to be out here," local resident Ryan Cutler, who used a drone to capture close-up photos of this year's spawning event (see below), told CBC News. "It's a really, really spectacular time to be around."

The cloud of milt arguably looks even more imposing up close, as you can see in this drone photo from resident Ryan Cutler, who described the spawning event as "fabulous" and "spectacular."

Spawning events can last anywhere between a few hours and several days, and scientists are increasingly turning to satellite images to help monitor these occurrences, according to the Earth Observatory. In this case, the milt cloud was visible for around 48 hours.

While the milky substance appears a striking green in these images, it is actually white. It appears green only because it is closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, meaning that less reflected light is absorbed by the water. This is also why shallow patches of water often appear turquoise when viewed from above.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The coastline alongside Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it strikes the perfect balance between a number of important factors. "Herrings prefer spawning locations that are more protected, have rocky substrate, and allow them to select areas with reduced salinity," Jessica Moffatt, a biologist with Vancouver Island's Island Marine Aquatic Working Group, told the Earth Observatory. "Barkley Sound hits the 'sweet spot' in many of these regards."

The Pacific herring is an important species in this region; it is a primary food source for Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), which give Salmon Beach its name. The herring are also hunted by local First Nation groups, according to CBC News.

During the spawning events, a wide range of other predatory marine life — including large fish, whales and sea lions — are drawn to the area to feast on the herring, according to the Earth Observatory. And on land, eagles, wolves and bears are more likely to appear during the mass reproduction event.

The milt appears green from above due to how wavelengths are absorbed by water as light reflects off the the white substance.

Coincidentally, this exact patch of ocean was the site of one of the weirdest oceanographic events ever seen. In 2020, around 4 miles (7 km) off the coast of Ucluelet (located just along the coastline to the left in the photo), scientists detected a rogue wave that appeared in the open ocean seemingly from nowhere. The massive wave reached the height of a four-story building, making it the most extreme version of this phenomenon ever seen.

Farther offshore, around 150 miles (240 km) south of Vancouver Island, researchers also detected a surprise swarm of more than 2,000 underwater earthquakes in a single day in March 2024, hinting that a section of the seafloor was ripping apart.

A recent satellite photo captured a gleaming halo of phytoplankton encircling the remote Chatham Islands. The stunning sight is the result of a hidden underwater structure, which has also helped kill hundreds of cetaceans.

#6510. Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

The more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions. Though our current search for potentially habitable worlds is mostly restricted to finding rocky planets with liquid water and atmospheres, it will have to advance well beyond that to bear fruit. Things like exoplanet plate tectonics to keep climates moderate, and stars with long, stable lifetimes that let life fluorish and evolve are factors in habitability.

New research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains. The research is titled "Raising mountains for a habitable Earth," and it's published in Science Advances. The lead author is Dr. Matthijs Smit of the University of British Columbiaâs Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences.

Their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes important chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere. That, in turn, led to the eventual appearance of complex life.

"The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability," the authors write.

K2 is the second tallest mountain in the world. The crust underneath it is some of the thickest in the world. Research shows that in Earth's past, the crust thickened in some places, leading to the growth of very tall mountains. Increased weathering from those mountains preceded the planet's episodes of oxygenation, and researchers hypothesize that episodic spurts of mountain growth enabled Earth's habitability, and the eventual appearance of complex life. Image Credit: By Zacharie Grossen - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/42469860

"Continental silicate weathering controls the oceanward flux of carbon and bioactive nutrients that limit marine primary productivity, thus exerting control on atmospheric chemistry, climate, and marine biomass and biodiversity," they explain. "The majority of the global terrigenous runoff derives from mountainous regions."

The researchers focused on the last three billion years of Earth's history. They examined metamorphic rocks that were pushed deep underground by overlying tectonic plates. When mountains formed where plates collided, the mountains were able to reach much greater heights. That raised nutrient levels in the oceans, which helped photosynthesizing lifeforms oxygenate Earth's atmosphere.

âChanges that occurred deep in the Earth ultimately gave rise to much taller mountains over time, which may have made our planet habitable by providing the nutrients needed for life to form and flourish,â lead author Smit said. âNutrients such as phosphorous are essential ingredients for life on our planet, but prior to three billion years ago, these elements were locked in the Earthâs crust and the oceans were quite nutrient-starved. All this changed when tall mountains started to develop.â

The research shows that two periods of peak metamorphic pressure inside the planet, between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, led to thicker crusts in mountain-forming regions, and that let taller mountains form. The growth of Earth's mountains spiked, and those orogenic growth spurts were synchronous with other important changes on the planet.

âThe first growth spurt may have led to the emergence of land on a large scale for the first time, while the second growth spurt thrust mountain ranges to enormous heights,â said co-author Dr. Douwe van Hinsbergen of Utrecht University, The Netherlands. âGiven such profound effects, mountains may well have played a far greater role in the creation of a habitable planet than previously assumed.â

Earth's atmospheric oxygen rose in distinct periods, and the most well-known and consequential one was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) from about 2.4 to 2.0 billion years ago. The researchers say that by the time the GOE occurred, Earth's mountains had grown substantially. They rose from near sea-level to about half the height of the modern-day Himalayas. Another distinct period of rising atmospheric oxygen was the Neoproterozoic Oxygen Event (NOE) from around 700 million to 500 million years ago. Mountain growth spiked at that time, too, according to the researchers. Various other atmospheric factors and oceanic factors related to habitability and complex life increased, too.

This figure shows time on the x-axis and more other information throughout. Blue shows how atmospheric O2 pressure rose compared to modern levels, especially during the GOE and the NOE. Purple shows the rise of sulfur isotope diversity, a measure of biological sulfur metabolism over time, and grey shows the percentage of oceanic strontium that comes from continental mountain erosion. Green shows the rise of organisms capable of oxygenic photosynthesis. The snowflake symbols show Earth's main icehouse stages. Image Credit: Smit et al. Science Advances 13 Nov 2026 Vol 12, Issue 46

The timing of these spurts of mountain growth coincided with the growth of crustal thickness in mountain belts. In these belts, the thickness of the upper accreted crust grows as plates collide. The first episode increased thickness from 30km to 60 km, and the second episode saw an increase to almost 90 km. âWe suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,â Dr. Smit said. âAs a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.â

"Causes for environmental upheaval culminating in the GOE and NOE have been sought in various external forcing mechanisms, such as increased runoff resulting from supercontinent breakup, enhanced weathering of basaltic rocks at low latitude, and a dwindling CO2 (carbon dioxide) flux from arc volcanism," the authors write. While the researchers agree that these are valid hypotheses, they also point out that they're transient. That doesn't match the "irreversible nature of global oxygenation," and other changes. They're also not restricted to periods preceding the GOE and NOE.

The two episodes of crustal thickening and resulting spikes in mountain elevation and erosion are a better fit. "In contrast to all of these processes, the orogenic growth associated with tectonic revolutions R1 and R2 broadly coincide with the major periods of environmental upheaval in terms of their approximate timing, paucity, and irreversibility," the authors write.

The researchers couldn't measure the height of long-gone mountains, but they were able to determine the density and thickness of ancient crust. Since crustal thickness and density correlate with mountain height, they could calculate the height of ancient mountains.

Earth's tallest mountains today, Mount Everest, K2 and Kangchenjunga, are almost certainly some of the tallest ever produced. They approach nine km above sea level, and the crust under them is about 80 km thick. That's twice as thick as other continents. They illustrate how crustal thickness generates tall mountains, and emphasize the hypothesis that mountain growth helped enable Earth's habitability.

âItâs likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,â said co-author Dr. Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm. âItâs exciting to think that mountain belts were once non-existent and that their development over the past three billion years may have driven the environmental and biological change that shaped our planet.â

#6509. New Once-Daily Pill Slashes Bad Cholesterol by Nearly 65% in Clinical Trial

A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

High cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

Enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

By blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57.1% to 64.6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

In a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

The review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

Enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

While clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

Reference: “Enlicitide: The First Oral PCSK9i for Lowering Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol” by Rachel C. Lucas, Mia E. Lussier, Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi and Taylor M. Clark, 14 October 2026, Annals of Pharmacotherapy. DOI: 10.1177/10600280261494015

#6508. Space Entrepreneurs Should Look To 16th Century Spice Trade For Inspiration

Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

But as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â

And even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

By 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

To that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

Iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he says.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

Over the past 30 years, NASAâs plans for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, says Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this new ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.

#6506. A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac

A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.

A new review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants, so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real-world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six studies followed participants for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects, and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing, or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.
