#6481. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly transform the brain — yet science is only beginning to understand how that transformation can affect a mother's mental health.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank.

That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths.

For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. That knowledge of what is normal is exactly what lets us recognize and treat what is not, from gestational diabetes to preeclampsia. But the brain, one of the most important organs in the human body, was left out altogether.

It wasn't until 2016 that my colleagues and I published the first study showing that pregnancy profoundly and measurably changes the structure of the human brain. That finding, which we described in the journal Nature Neuroscience, became the seed of my lab. In the years since, a remarkable picture has emerged. The brain changes associated with pregnancy and the postpartum phase are more pronounced, or at least occur more rapidly, than those of adolescence — the transformation we usually treat as the epitome of a remodeling brain.

Today, neuroscientists consider the months of pregnancy and the postpartum period to be one of the most plastic periods for the adult brain. These changes are dynamic; some regions shrink in volume during gestation and grow after birth, while others follow the opposite pattern. They are driven by hormones, tracking with the enormous swings in estrogens and other hormones across pregnancy. And they are long-lasting — some of these structural changes persist for years, and preliminary evidence suggests they may last decades. Or, as folk wisdom has long put it, once a mother, always a mother.

For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank.

These findings raise a question I'm asked constantly: Are these brain changes behind the phenomenon of "mommy brain," sometimes called "momnesia"? It is an effect many women report, and it deserves a careful accounting of its possible causes — among them sleep deprivation and the enormous mental and metabolic load of gestating and raising a human being. We are still investigating, but the data so far point in a reassuring direction: These brain changes are not associated with worse cognitive functioning. If anything, it's the opposite: We have evidence that the women whose brains changed the most were the ones who reported greater well-being and, in turn, an easier time bonding with their newborns.

But not every change is benign. The same plasticity that helps a mother adapt can also carry risk. In one of our most recent studies, published in the journal Science Advances in 2025, we found that certain brain changes were associated with a greater rise in depressive symptoms during the postpartum period. And here is the other side of the coin: A highly plastic brain is also a vulnerable one.

During pregnancy and the postpartum period, that same capacity for change makes the brain more susceptible to disturbances. The window that should lead to learning and bonding, for some women, opens onto suffering instead — especially when society fails to support them, when it doesn't recognize this period as a stage in which women need protection and support from their families and institutions.

The brain changes during pregnancy and the postpartum period are more pronounced and rapid than those that take place during adolescence.

The epidemiological data are as alarming as the personal stories behind them. Roughly 1 in 5 women will experience perinatal depression. In developed countries, suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. Let me say that again, because it bears repeating: Suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. And what happens to a mother's mental health does not stay with her — it ripples out to the well-being of her baby, her family and society as a whole. Advancing maternal mental health is urgent, and the first step is to generate the high-quality data that will let us truly understand the brain transformation that accompanies pregnancy and the postpartum period — to describe what happens to mothers on the basis of science, not personal opinion, inherited prejudice or incomplete medical models.

It is a serious problem, but the solution is straightforward ‪—‬ especially now, in the age of artificial intelligence. The tools of modern data science are extraordinarily powerful, but they are hungry ‪—‬ they need large, high-quality, deeply characterized datasets to learn from and make predictions. In maternal brain health, those datasets do not yet exist. We have blood biobanks from pregnancy, neuroimaging from postpartum parents, questionnaires on bonding, records on breastfeeding — but they sit in separate silos, captured at different moments, never integrated. No resource follows the same women from before conception, through pregnancy, and years past birth, linking biofluids, neuroimaging, neuropsychological assessments, and the social conditions of their lives.

Building that resource should be a priority for anyone who cares about women's health. It is the kind of infrastructure that transformed other fields. Databases like the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative for Alzheimer's disease and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study for adolescence turned scattered observations into predictive science. Motherhood deserves the same — not a footnote appended to the study of something else. It deserves its own chapter — its own public, longitudinal, well-characterized database, spanning from molecules to societies.

For the past nine years, my lab's efforts have focused on laying the groundwork for such a database, and we now have hundreds of participants assessed before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and in the postpartum period. But hundreds is not enough. To do this science properly, we need to scale from hundreds of women to thousands and to ensure, as much as possible, adequate geographic and social representation. My role within initiatives like ENIGMA-Neuroendocrinology and the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative is to coordinate with other outstanding researchers to reach that goal with the highest quality and the greatest urgency we can manage.

None of this requires a scientific miracle. It requires a decision to treat the maternal brain as something worth studying with the same rigor and the same resources we devote to every other domain of biomedicine. For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank. What we need is the collective will, and the sustained funding, to finish the picture.

If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org.

Eighty-five percent of women experience pregnancy at some point in their lives. It enables the very existence of our species. Yet this first step in the process of nurturing the next generation has had little serious, rigorous study — until now.

Susana Carmona's A Mother’s Brain is a landmark in ending sexual bias in women's health. Among her many initiatives, she is building a unique longitudinal database tracking how mothers’ brains change from preconception to several years after childbirth.

Susana Carmona is the author of "A Mother's Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution" (The MIT Press). Carmona is the founder of Neuromaternal, a lab based in Madrid, and is a mother herself. Her research has been referenced across popular media from the CBS sitcom "The Big Bang Theory" to the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, National Geographic, Smithsonian, and Mother Jones.

#6476. A Chemical Signature Suddenly Disappeared From Earth’s Rocks. Scientists Think They Know Why

Scientists have uncovered a mysterious chemical change in ancient rocks that reveals a major turning point in Earth’s geological history.

A chemical fingerprint preserved in some of Earth’s oldest rocks disappears from the geological record around 2.5 billion years ago. Researchers at Curtin University have traced this abrupt change across thousands of rock samples, identifying a major transition in how Earth’s crust formed and recycled. Their findings suggest that the planet was beginning to develop a tectonic system resembling the one operating today.

Determining when plate tectonics emerged has been a longstanding challenge. The movement of Earth’s tectonic plates continually reshapes continents and ocean basins, while recycling enormous amounts of crust into the planet’s interior. This process destroys much of the geological evidence needed to reconstruct its earliest history.

The researchers investigated chemical signatures that can survive when older crust melts and contributes to the formation of new rock. These signatures can help identify the original material from which younger rocks formed.

“New crust often forms by melting older rock, leaving behind a distinctive chemical fingerprint,” said lead author Dr. Janne Liebmann, a research fellow at Curtin University. “We searched for this fingerprint in thousands of rocks from around the world, spanning almost four billion years of Earth’s history.”

“We found it consistently in rocks older than 2.5 billion years, showing they were derived from a pool of ancient crust that formed about four billion years ago.”

“But after 2.5 billion years ago, that fingerprint disappears from the geological record, and despite examining thousands of rocks, we never see it again.”

The disappearance suggests that the processes responsible for generating new crust underwent a fundamental transformation. Rather than repeatedly melting and reworking ancient crust in place, Earth increasingly developed a system capable of transporting and recycling crust across much larger distances.

“That tells us something fundamental changed in the way Earth’s crust was being formed and transformed, marking a transition towards the dynamic tectonic system we see today,” Liebmann said.

Study co-author Professor Chris Kirkland, from Curtin’s School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, connected the findings to the geological processes that distinguish Earth from planets such as Venus and Mars, which lack a comparable global system of active plate tectonics.

“Plate tectonics is fundamental to the way Earth has evolved over billions of years, continually reshaping the continents and oceans and influencing the planet’s atmosphere and climate,” Kirkland said.

“What makes this finding remarkable is that we can see the fingerprints of an ancient Earth disappear from the geological record at a very specific point in time.”

“It marks the transition from an early Earth where ancient crust could be repeatedly melted and reworked in place, to a system capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale.”

The results identify a major change in crustal evolution around 2.5 billion years ago, although they do not establish that modern plate tectonics began suddenly or that all its defining features emerged simultaneously.

“This gives us our clearest geological evidence yet for when the tectonic engine that drives the modern Earth ‘switched on’.”

Reference: “Loss of ancient crustal reservoirs marks a shift in Earth’s geodynamic regime” by Janne Liebmann, Christopher L. Kirkland, Michael I. H. Hartnady and Christopher J. Spencer, 1 November 2026, Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences. DOI: 10.1098/rspa.2026.0587

#6474. A Billion-Year-Old Rift Could Be Hiding a Vast Energy Source—And Prospectors Are Already Digging In

Underground hydrogen gas could feed data centers’ big hunger for electricity.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Scattered sparsely across Earth’s surface, from Nebraska to Mali to the Philippines, drilling rigs are rising from platforms surrounded by sheds and tanks. Each contains a tower 10 to 15 stories high. Only they aren’t pumping fossil fuels. While they’re reminiscent of machinery used to extract oil and gas, these rigs are on the hunt for a different type of gas—one trapped in microscopic pores of rock—that some researchers believe could help solve humanity’s clean energy needs for hundreds of years. Or at least offset our ever-increasing demand.

Natural stores of hydrogen gas exist throughout our planet’s crust on every continent. It’s colorless and odorless, and it frequently escapes into the atmosphere through natural seeps or during mining for metals like copper and zinc. But finding it in commercially viable quantities has always been difficult. Now, researchers and entrepreneurs think they have reason to hope this challenge can be overcome.

“There are places where we believe we’re going to find natural hydrogen accumulations, and in those places it’s going to be a very competitive energy source,” says Pete Johnson, CEO and cofounder of hydrogen exploration company Koloma. The company plans to drill 20 wells in the next two years in some of “the best hydrogen systems” in the world, including in the U.S. and the Philippines.

Hydrogen is already a multibillion-dollar global industry. Fertilizer companies combine it with nitrogen to make ammonia. Oil refineries use it to lower the sulfur content in diesel. Metalworkers use it to prevent oxidation. Hydrogen is “an essential element for survival of humanity,” says Ukrainian geochemist Viacheslav Zgonnik, PhD. But nearly all of the hydrogen used in those processes is manufactured, and much of it from methane gas in an energy-intensive way. So energy intensive, in fact, that companies produce 9 to 11 tons of carbon dioxide for every 1 ton of hydrogen, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute.

Some companies are exploring ways to produce hydrogen with fewer carbon emissions. But even so-called green hydrogen still requires energy to produce and may never be economically viable at scale, says Zgonnik. That’s where natural hydrogen deposits enter the picture. And scientists and prospectors believe natural hydrogen could serve far more industries than just fertilizer and petroleum production. Some even envision it could help power the world with near-zero carbon emissions in the process.

Exactly how much hydrogen exists, however, is still up for debate. A 2024 U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) paper modeled the amount of hydrogen likely to percolate under the surface and found enormous amounts. The bulk is likely “impractical to recover,” according to the paper published in Science Advances, but if even a small fraction of the total amount could be captured, it “would supply the projected hydrogen needed to reach net-zero emissions for [about] 200 years.”

A 2025 report from The Royal Society was more cautious, tempering the optimism of the USGS model by using currently available hydrogen survey data. But even that suggested hydrogen “could be a game changer.”

Hydrogen forms naturally through at least two processes: chemical reactions between water and iron-rich rocks, and the splitting of water molecules by radiation in rocks containing uranium, according to the Royal Society paper. The gas then saturates porous rock, akin to an underground sponge sealed on the top by a dense layer of caprock such as clay or other sedimentary rocks. Stick a straw—or in practical terms a drill—into the sponge, and out comes the hydrogen.

Known hydrogen accumulations occur in the oldest and most stable rocks on Earth at the core of the continents. Researchers speculate it exists in places where Earth’s crust tried to separate, like the Midcontinent Rift, which stretches beneath portions of Kansas, Iowa, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, and the Great Rift Valley in eastern Africa. The gas has also been found in regions where tectonic plates collided, including parts of the Pacific Rim off the coasts of North America and Asia, says Canadian hydrogen researcher Barbara Sherwood Lollar, PhD.

But natural underground hydrogen, also called gold or white hydrogen, has been discovered in plenty of other locations, too. In Mali, a country in western Africa, drillers searching for fresh water discovered a natural hydrogen system. Decades later, the Bourakebougou field, as it is called, began to produce enough hydrogen to supply electricity to a nearby village.

Local supplies of natural hydrogen could be among the gas’s first and most practical applications, says Lollar, who has studied natural hydrogen for decades, one of the few early researchers investigating hydrogen as a potential source for clean energy. In May, she coauthored a paper in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences detailing how more than 70 percent of the continental crust “has the potential for hydrogen generation.” That widespread distribution, she says, could make the gas a source of local and regional power.

“Another one of the easy wins in all of this would be to use this hydrogen not just for a small community,” says Sherwood Lollar, a University of Toronto professor. “The same rocks that produce hydrogen and helium are the rocks that produce nickel, copper, gold, diamonds, critical minerals.” That means mining conglomerates could capture hydrogen already being vented and use it to power their facilities.

Johnson takes the idea a step further. Industries that require large amounts of power, such as data centers, or industries that require hydrogen, like fertilizer manufacturers, could relocate to places where natural hydrogen is abundant, reducing the need to transport the gas.

Companies like Koloma are already surveying for economically viable deposits around the world. Johnson says his company has identified several potential fields.

Assuming the hydrogen reservoirs are large enough to economically produce, the process would look much like drilling for natural gas, he says. The timeline for developing the industry could be similar, too.

“We’re in some early innings right now,” Johnson says. “I mean if you look at how long it took us to develop the concept of shale gas, that was a 20- to 30-year process.”

Then a few years after companies began drilling successful wells, the shale gas industry boomed. Natural hydrogen could follow a similar trajectory. Some companies are also exploring ways to stimulate hydrogen production underground by injecting heat and water into rocks before extracting the resulting gas. Those efforts, however, remain in their infancy.

Natural hydrogen could do more than help satisfy humanity’s insatiable appetite for energy—made worse by the buildout of energy-hungry data centers. It could also reshape the global energy map.

“If the Philippines, for example, has domestic energy, what it means is that its neighboring countries like Taiwan, Japan, all these energy-poor countries may also have it,” Johnson says. “Anytime you find a new energy source in new places, it sort of rewrites the rules of geopolitics.”

He’s not certain exactly what role the gas will play in the world’s future energy portfolio. Will it render oil and gas obsolete, or will it become no more than a bit player? “That’s the question we’re trying to answer.”

First, researchers and prospectors need to hunt down untapped hydrogen reservoirs and prove that they’re worth drilling.

#6472. A Century-Old Pollution Disaster Has Been Discovered Frozen in Arctic Ice

Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.

More than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source. Much of that contamination went unmeasured at the time, but traces of it survived in an unexpected place: Arctic ice.

Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead. The findings also demonstrate how the Earth’s ice preserves evidence of human activity long after pollution has disappeared from the air.

The study, published November 10 in Nature Sustainability, was led by Joe McConnell and Nathan Chellman of the Desert Research Institute (DRI), alongside international collaborators. The team examined 10 ice cores from Greenland, northern Canada, and the Russian Arctic, finding that concentrations of toxic metals in some locations rose to approximately 15 times preindustrial levels between 1886 and 1918.

The evidence pointed to the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, one of the world’s largest copper producers at the time. Researchers estimated that during its peak production decades, the operation released approximately 11,000 tons of arsenic and 4,400 tons of lead into the atmosphere each year.

“It’s pretty wild to think that a single, albeit massive source of pollution could have affected effectively the entire North American continent and western Greenland more than 4000 kilometers or 2500 miles away,” McConnell said.

Using historical census records and models of atmospheric pollution, the researchers estimated that approximately 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic concentrations associated with increased risks of lung cancer and other serious illnesses.

People living near the operation faced particularly high exposure. For nearly 30 years, residents of Montana and parts of Wyoming and Idaho experienced arsenic concentrations that met or exceeded the World Health Organization’s current recommended maximum threshold for chronic exposure. The researchers also estimated that 1.4 million Americans and Canadians encountered elevated lead pollution potentially associated with cognitive effects equivalent to a 2.6-point reduction in IQ.

Although the study did not directly measure health outcomes, arsenic and lead exposure are associated with cancer, diabetes, cognitive decline, and heart disease. Pollution settling onto crops, soil, and water could also have created additional risks beyond those examined in the study.

To reconstruct this forgotten pollution, scientists turned to the Arctic’s natural record of atmospheric change. As snow accumulates, it traps tiny particles carried by the wind, including industrial pollutants. Over time, the snow becomes ice, preserving chemical evidence of conditions from decades or even centuries earlier.

By comparing metal concentrations across the 10 ice cores, combining them with atmospheric models, and examining historical mining records, the researchers traced the contamination to northern North America. Arsenic measurements, supported by related chemical markers, closely matched Anaconda’s production history, while lead isotope evidence reinforced the connection.

The timing also revealed how industrial decisions shaped the atmosphere. Copper demand surged during rapid electrification and the buildup to World War I, increasing pollution from ore processing. Near Anaconda, damaged crops, reduced harvests, and livestock deaths had already prompted decades of legal disputes.

After the company installed pollution-control equipment around 1919, heavy-metal emissions declined by approximately 65%, according to the ice-core evidence. Similar technology had been available years earlier, but Anaconda delayed installation for roughly a decade.

The researchers calculated that installing those controls ten years sooner could have prevented another 60,000 tons of arsenic and 24,000 tons of lead from spreading across much of North America.

The Arctic record captures both sides of that history. It reveals how pollution from one industrial site reached millions of people and how changes in industrial practices eventually reduced its impact. Even today, the ice preserves evidence of environmental damage that otherwise might have remained largely hidden.

Reference: “Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early twentieth century copper production” by Joseph R. McConnell, Nathan J. Chellman, Sophie M. Wensman, Alison S. Criscitiello, Andreas Plach, Dorthe Dahl-Jensen, Diedrich Fritzsche, Kira M. Holland, Drake McCrimmon, Matthew B. Osman, John Sandlos and Andreas Stohl, 10 November 2026, Nature Sustainability. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9

A factory worker experimented with a pressurized air system while on the job, and it resulted in a fatal injury.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 35-year-old man in the Czech Republic

The symptoms: The man was injured while working in a factory. His co-workers learned he'd been hurt after he crawled from the ground floor to the first floor and shouted for help. He had severe abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, and he said he had been injured while conducting "a silly experiment" involving a pressurized air system. However, he did not describe exactly what had happened.

"He repeatedly stressed that the incident was his own fault," doctors later wrote in a report of his case.

What happened next: The man was flown by helicopter to a nearby hospital, but during the flight, he became unresponsive and showed signs of hemorrhagic shock — a type of shock caused by significant blood loss over a short period. Shock, broadly, is when organs and body tissues don't receive enough oxygen due to decreased blood flow; if untreated, it can lead to organ failure and death.

Medical attendants in the helicopter worked to revive the man, but he died before he could be admitted to the hospital. Because the fatal injury occurred at the man's workplace, the police ordered a medicolegal autopsy, which both identifies the cause of death and collects details for law enforcement agencies, as part of an inquest procedure.

The autopsy: The coroner examined the body and noted that the soft tissues of the man's face were swollen and abnormally distended from retained air. The man's anus and genital areas were similarly distended and densely coated with dried blood, with radial tears in the skin surrounding the anus.

Next, the coroner conducted an internal examination. The man's brain was swollen, and he had air bubbles in his brain and chest cavity. Blood had collected around his diaphragm (the large muscle that helps inflate and deflate the lungs). It had also accumulated in the wall between the heart chambers on the left side, in tubes leading to his lungs, and in the membranes covering his lungs and heart. Reservoirs of blood also pooled in the man's abdominal cavity, in the tube leading to his right kidney, and in his digestive organs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The man's heart was "shrunken and empty," according to the report.

The autopsy also revealed foreign objects stuck between loops of the man's small intestine. These included three pieces of a black rubber pipe stopper and scraps of a plastic bag. His rectum — the final straight portion of the large intestine — had detached violently from his anus. It was surrounded by blood and marked with a laceration that was nearly circular, indicating that an "explosive rectal injury" had triggered hemorrhagic shock and caused the man's death, the coroner concluded.

Further investigation: Additional evidence from the factory and rubber fragments in the man's small intestine provided the police with further insight into his injuries; additional clues came from his internet search history, including photos of himself that he'd submitted to an amateur sex website.

The police concluded that the man had been performing autoerotic anal stimulation while at work, using a rubber inflatable pipe stopper measuring 2 to 3 inches (50 to 70 millimeters) in diameter, and an air gun, a handheld device for directing powerful jets of compressed air.

They suggested that the man likely attached the expandable pipe stopper to the muzzle of the air gun, which was in turn connected to the factory's air distribution system by a long, high-pressure hose. He then covered the pipe stopper with a plastic bag, inserted it into his rectal cavity, and pressed the air gun's trigger, causing "an unexpected abrupt inflation and explosive bursting of the pipe stopper within his rectum," the doctors wrote in the case report.

What makes the case unique: This case is the first recorded example of a person dying from a "rectal explosion during self-gratification," the doctors wrote. Piecing together the circumstances leading up to the man's injury was important for the hospital's doctors and law enforcement to understand how the fatality likely occurred, the authors said.

When performed responsibly and consensually, rectal insertion of foreign bodies typically does not cause significant injury, the authors added. However, "the introduction of some objects into the rectum might have unpredictable and even fatal effects."

#6470. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6468. Scientists Catch Water Molecules Breaking Apart Before Their Electrons Can Respond

When X-rays strike a water molecule, the molecule can break apart faster than its electrons can complete a fundamental relaxation process. Scientists have discovered that both bonds holding hydrogen to oxygen can rupture within just a few femtoseconds, leaving behind an excited, electrically neutral oxygen atom.

The discovery challenges established interpretations of how water responds to X-ray radiation. It also identifies a previously overlooked source of highly reactive atomic oxygen, which can participate in further chemical reactions.

When a water molecule absorbs a sufficiently energetic X-ray photon, an electron can be ejected from an inner shell of its oxygen atom. The resulting vacancy normally triggers Auger decay, a rapid process in which another electron fills the vacancy and transfers enough energy to eject a second electron.

However, the researchers found that the molecular structure can change even faster. The particular electronic state produced by X-ray absorption creates strong repulsive forces, allowing both oxygen-hydrogen bonds to break before Auger decay occurs.

“What makes this result particularly exciting is that we see the molecule break apart before the electronic relaxation has even finished. Both O–H bonds rupture within the lifetime of the oxygen core hole, so the nuclear motion is essentially winning the race against the electrons,” explained Florian Trinter of FHI in Berlin.

The team examined isolated water molecules in the gas phase using high-resolution electron spectroscopy at two synchrotron facilities: PETRA III at DESY in Hamburg, Germany, and the FlexPES beamline at MAX IV in Lund, Sweden.

Both experiments detected unusually sharp peaks at specific electron energies. These features could not be explained by the electronic decay of intact water molecules or the molecular fragments typically expected after X-ray absorption.

“Seeing the characteristic signal also at MAX IV was an important part of establishing this as a genuine molecular fragmentation pathway. The measurements at the two facilities give us a very consistent picture of what happens to the water molecule after X-ray excitation,” said Gunnar Öhrwall of MAX IV in Lund.

To determine what produced the unusual electron signals, the researchers performed detailed molecular and atomic calculations. The predicted electron energies matched the decay of excited neutral oxygen atoms rather than hydroxyl (OH) fragments.

This distinction matters because the energies of emitted electrons depend on the electronic structure of the atom or molecule producing them. The exceptionally narrow spectral features provided a recognizable signature of oxygen that had already separated from the original water molecule.

“The energy of the emitted electrons provides a kind of fingerprint of the state that is formed. Our calculations show that the observed features are consistent with the decay of an excited neutral oxygen atom that has already separated from the water molecule,” explained Ludger Inhester of CFEL at DESY in Hamburg.

The results offer a new explanation for high-energy electron features observed in earlier water experiments. Signals previously associated with hydroxyl fragments may instead originate from excited neutral oxygen atoms produced through extremely rapid molecular fragmentation.

Because neutral atomic oxygen is highly reactive, understanding how it forms could improve models of chemical processes initiated by X-ray radiation. The findings also provide a more precise basis for interpreting electron spectra from water and related molecular systems.

Reference: “Ultrafast Dissociation of Water Producing Atomic Oxygen following Excitation above the O 1s Threshold” by Florian Trinter, Stephan Thürmer, Qi Zhou (周琪), Uwe Hergenhahn, Bernd Winter, Olle Björneholm, Maxim Tchaplyguine, Ludger Inhester and Gunnar Öhrwall, 5 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/c1hm-82p2

#6467. Just 2 Weeks of Ultraprocessed Foods May Change How Your Brains Respond to Food

Just two weeks of eating ultraprocessed foods may be enough to alter how the developing brain responds to rewarding foods. In a Virginia Tech study, adults ages 18 to 21 showed reduced activity in a brain region involved in food rewards and decision-making after following a diet rich in ultraprocessed products. Participants aged 22 to 25 showed no significant changes.

“Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” said Emma Leslie, the study’s first author. The findings, published in the journal Obesity, suggest that sensitivity to ultraprocessed foods may vary even within a relatively narrow age range.

The orbitofrontal cortex helps the brain evaluate rewards, make decisions, and regulate eating behavior. It is also among the last brain regions to fully mature, with development continuing into the mid to late 20s. “The orbitofrontal cortex is still undergoing development in all of our participants, but the younger you are, the more rapid the development,” said neuroscientist Alex DiFeliceantonio of Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC. “It’s also an area of the brain that has been shown to be active in people who are dieting or who are trying to reduce their craving for high-calorie foods.”

The brain findings build on earlier results from the same experiment. Researchers previously found that participants ages 18 to 21 consumed more calories after following the ultraprocessed diet, even when they were not hungry. Older participants did not show the same pattern. “This was especially interesting given our previous findings showing that younger participants also consumed more calories at a buffet-style meal after the ultraprocessed diet,” Leslie said. “Together, these findings raise interesting questions about whether certain developmental periods may be particularly sensitive to ultraprocessed food exposure.”

To investigate the effects of food processing, researchers recruited 22 adults ages 18 to 25, including seven who were 21 or younger. Each participant completed two dietary interventions lasting two weeks each, separated by a four-week break. The order of the diets was randomly assigned.

One diet contained no ultraprocessed foods, while the other supplied 81 percent of calories from ultraprocessed products. Both provided identical proportions of carbohydrates (50 percent), fat (35 percent), and protein (15 percent). Researchers also matched fiber, added sugar, saturated fat, sodium, energy density, and overall nutritional quality. Calorie intake was adjusted to maintain each participant’s weight, allowing the team to examine the effects of food processing without major differences in nutritional composition or weight change.

Before and after each dietary period, participants underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in blood oxygenation associated with brain activity. During the scans, a pump delivered either a highly processed milkshake or a tasteless solution through a straw-like device. Among younger participants, the orbitofrontal cortex responded less strongly to the milkshake after the ultraprocessed diet, but its response increased after the diet without ultraprocessed foods. Neither diet produced significant changes in the older group.

Because the diets were closely matched nutritionally, conventional measures of dietary quality did not readily explain the observed differences. “The diets were matched on macronutrients, energy density, and micronutrients, so it’s something other than nutrition that is leading to changes in the brain and behavior,” DiFeliceantonio said. “Could it be additives? Chemicals produced during the processing itself? It’s an open question.”

Ultraprocessed foods often contain industrially manufactured ingredients or additives that are uncommon in home kitchens. Researchers have not determined whether particular ingredients, processing methods, or combinations of factors explain the brain changes observed in this trial. In the United States, ultraprocessed products account for more than half of young adults’ diets. Their consumption has also been associated with metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular problems, and other health conditions, although such associations do not establish that processing itself causes those outcomes.

The orbitofrontal cortex is involved not only in evaluating food rewards but also in decisions that can influence when someone stops eating. “This study is important because you have this change in an area of the brain known to govern self-control and potentially put a stop to eating,” DiFeliceantonio said. “This is giving us insight into how ultraprocessed foods are affecting the bodies and brains of younger people, who might be especially vulnerable to their effects. And that’s important to know for things like dietary guidelines, doctor recommendations, and policy decisions.”

However, the researchers found no association between participants’ diet-related changes in brain responses and changes in how much they ate. Although younger adults showed differences in both measures, the study did not establish that altered orbitofrontal activity caused increased calorie consumption. The neurological and behavioral effects could involve separate or overlapping mechanisms that require further investigation.

The study included only 22 participants, and just seven belonged to the younger age group. The age-related findings were exploratory, meaning they were identified through analyses that require confirmation in larger studies. Researchers also cannot yet determine whether the observed brain changes persist, reverse after dietary changes, or influence eating habits over longer periods.

“The intervention lasted only two weeks, so we don’t know whether these changes persist over time or translate into long-term differences in eating behavior,” Leslie said. Future experiments will need to examine whether the effects remain after participants resume their usual diets and whether similar changes occur consistently across larger and more diverse populations.

DiFeliceantonio and Virginia Tech nutrition researcher Brenda Davy hope to extend their work to people younger than 18, whose brains are undergoing more rapid development. “In the U.S., adolescents have the poorest overall dietary quality and consume more ultraprocessed foods than any other age group,” Davy said. “Dietary habits are established early in life and typically persist into adulthood. We hope to continue to study how highly processed foods affect young people’s eating habits and health, which ultimately could impact dietary guidelines for this age group.”

Leslie, who completed her doctorate at Virginia Tech and continued her research as a postdoctoral associate at the University of Michigan, is also examining how ultraprocessed foods influence reward-related behavior. “I’ll be investigating the addictive potential of ultraprocessed foods and exploring food policy strategies to address challenges in the modern food environment,” Leslie said. “Ultimately, I hope this work will help identify who may be most vulnerable, why, and how we can better support healthier eating behaviors.”

Reference: “Effects of Controlled Diets High in and Free of Ultraprocessed Food on the Brain of Emerging Adults” by Emma H. Leslie, Maria L. M. Rego, Monica Ahrens, Wenjing Yu, Mary Elizabeth Baugh, Anastasia Groccia, Rhianna M. Sullivan, Han Lee, Ryann Kolb, Delbert L. Herald, Collin Gregg, Valisa E. Hedrick, Kevin P. Davy, Benjamin Katz, Brenda M. Davy and Alexandra G. DiFeliceantonio, 18 November 2026, Obesity. DOI: 10.1002/oby.70341

The research was supported by a grant to DiFeliceantonio and Davy from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, part of the National Institutes of Health. Leslie was also supported with an exercise health sciences graduate fellowship from Dr. Ray A. Gaskins.

#6466. The Forever Chemicals Wreaking Havoc on Our Planet Are About to Meet Their Kryptonite

Your water filter traps forever chemicals but can’t destroy them. This new one can, if we can afford it.

One of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS. These man-made compounds show up in everything from non-stick pans to fast-food wrappers. They’re called “forever chemicals” because their carbon-fluorine bonds are so strong that they barely break down. The PFAS family includes nearly 15,000 different compounds, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, but the FDA tests food and animal feed for only a couple dozen of them.

Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.

One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters. Currently, filters can trap a variety of PFAS but can’t destroy them, meaning the filters basically just move the toxic chemicals from one place to another. However, a study in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences describes a filter that uses hydrogen to attack carbon-fluorine bonds. When tested against six PFAS of regulatory concern, it worked on all of them.

“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” Arizona State University’s Bruce Rittmann, the senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “We showed that this mechanism worked for all six. It’s a universal mechanism.”

Hydrogen is essential for this process because once activated into a reactive form, it drives a process known as “hydrodefluorination,” stripping and replacing the fluorine and forming carbon-hydrogen bonds. To activate that hydrogen, Rittman and his team used palladium nanoparticles that can convert the hydrogen gas into its much-needed reactive form.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann said in a press statement.

As hydrogen and PFAS travel through the membrane, both are attracted to the palladium catalyst. However, hydrogen isn’t simply added to the waste stream—instead, it’s fed directly into the membrane itself. This gives the filter the perfect opportunity to chemically dismantle those troublesome carbon-fluorine bonds. Over two months of continuous operation, the membrane broke apart most of the PFAS it captured. It removed 90 percent of the chemicals and stripped about 83 percent of their fluorine.

That’s a huge advancement for combating the proliferation of PFAS in the natural environment, but a big limitation will be cost. Simply put, palladium isn’t cheap, and Rittman estimates that roughly a kilogram of the stuff costs about $50,000. The new approach could be paired with conventional treatments, which would first concentrate the PFAS into a smaller waste stream that the palladium membrane could then destroy.

“Decades of extensive deployment of PFAS in firefighting foams, oil- and water-repellent surfaces, non-stick cookware, and food-contact materials have created diffuse, chronic inputs into watersheds and drinking-water supplies,” the authors wrote in the study. “Hydrogen-driven hydrodefluorination offers a direct reductive route under comparatively mild conditions.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6465. Scientists Discover That a Simple Change in Walking Habits Could Improve Blood Sugar Control

Scientists have discovered that a simple change in how daily exercise is distributed could improve blood sugar control, particularly in people at risk of type 2 diabetes.

How you distribute exercise throughout the day may influence how well your body regulates blood sugar. A randomized trial published in Obesity found that frequent, short walks improved several measures of glucose regulation more than completing the same amount of walking in one continuous session.

The differences emerged after six weeks, despite both groups performing similar amounts of physical activity and burning comparable amounts of energy.

Researchers recruited 30 inactive adults with overweight or obesity who reported sitting for more than six hours daily. Participants were assigned to complete 45 minutes of brisk walking five days per week for six weeks, either in one continuous session or in approximately five-minute breaks spread throughout the day.

Continuous glucose monitoring showed that the short-walk group increased its time within the target blood sugar range from 82% to 94%. In contrast, the continuous-walking group experienced a decline from 89% to 80%.

Participants taking frequent walking breaks also had more stable glucose levels, largely because they experienced fewer unusually low readings rather than lower average or peak blood sugar levels.

Laboratory tests showed that participants who took frequent walking breaks experienced more favorable changes in glucose tolerance, indicating differences in how their bodies cleared glucose from the bloodstream. However, neither approach produced a detectable improvement in insulin sensitivity.

Researchers suggest that repeated muscle activity may influence glucose uptake and utilization, although the exact mechanisms remain uncertain.

“Our findings suggest that how we distribute physical activity throughout the day may be just as important as how much we do,” said corresponding author Audrey Bergouignan, PhD, Director of Research at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Associate Professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. “Rather than relying solely on a single exercise session, regularly interrupting prolonged sitting with short walks may offer additional benefits for blood glucose regulation, especially in people at risk of developing type 2 diabetes.”

The findings suggest that interrupting prolonged sitting may offer glucose regulation benefits beyond those associated with total exercise duration.

However, the trial was small and lasted only six weeks. It also lacked a non-exercise control group, and participants’ diets were not controlled during glucose monitoring. Further research is needed to determine whether these improvements translate into long-term health benefits, particularly for people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.

Reference: “Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Improves Glucose Regulation More Than Continuous Walking in Adults With Overweight/Obesity” by Ana J. Pinto, Nathan P. De Jong, Josiane L. Broussard, Chantal Simon, Carlos Mendez, Andrew H. Lange, Laura Schreck, Zhaoxing Pan, Daniel H. Bessesen and Audrey Bergouignan, 18 November 2026, Obesity. DOI: 10.1002/oby.70349

A 2,000-year-old tomb was discovered in an elite burial ground of the Xiongnu, some of whom were the ancestors of the Huns.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia.

Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East.

When the Xiongnu Empire fractured in the late first century B.C., one band moved west, picking up new tribes and eventually becoming the horde known as the Huns. Both the Xiongnu and the Huns were well known for their fighting and horseback riding skills.

The newly announced tomb is roughly square, with a long passageway extending from it, according to the statement. Including the passageway, the tomb is about 240 feet (73 meters) long, roughly the size of the Great Sphinx of Giza. Archaeologists discovered nine concentric layers of stone, each smaller than the last, going down around 48 feet (14.5 m) deep, making the tomb a kind of inverted pyramid.

Jade "bi" discs unearthed on the floor of the coffin.

A glass cup with a handle, possibly made in the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists unearthed a wooden carriage from one of the tomb layers.

In the tomb's central chamber, archaeologists found a wooden burial chamber with a coffin. The burial chamber is smaller than other elite Xiongnu burials, according to the statement, which may suggest that the society was changing and Xiongnu power was declining when the tomb was created in the late first to second century A.D.

Artifacts found in the tomb show the extent of the Xiongnu's connections across Eurasia 2,000 years ago, according to the statement. Among the grave goods recovered from the tomb were silver-and-quartz accessories crafted to decorate horses, as well as a wheel from a lacquered horse-drawn carriage, suggesting the tomb's occupant was a person of high social status.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Additionally, archaeologists found evidence of connections with the Han dynasty, which arose around 200 B.C. and was the second imperial dynasty of ancient China. On the bottom of the wooden coffin, archaeologists recovered 15 flat, overlapping pieces of jade.

Han dynasty burials of important people often included at least one "bi," the term for a jade disk. But unlike the typically circular "bi," the jade pieces in the Xiongnu tomb are irregular and have elaborate designs engraved on them, according to the statement. This may suggest that the Xiongnu adopted a Han burial practice but put their own spin on it.

Archaeologists also found a broken cup in the tomb. The transparent glass cup with a handle may have been manufactured in the Roman Empire, the archaeologists believe. Additional tests will be carried out to try to determine where the glass cup was made.

So far, archaeologists are unsure who was buried in the tomb. But they plan to use DNA analysis techniques on the teeth and hair they recovered from the coffin to figure out the person's chromosomal sex and whether the individual was related to other people interred in the Duurlig Nars burial complex. According to the statement, future analyses of this important tomb will help archaeologists paint a more detailed picture of ancient Xiongnu society two millennia ago.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6463. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
